chapters.title: Mathematical models and graphing software
objectives: Translate a practical rule into a linear model
Use a spreadsheet or graphing tool to compare two models
Check a graphical solution against algebra and context
paragraphs: A mathematical model selects quantities and states assumptions. For a delivery charge, let x be distance in kilometres and C be cost in shillings. A fixed starting charge plus a constant charge per kilometre gives C=ax+b. The intercept b describes the starting charge; a has units shillings per kilometre. State whether fractional distances are allowed and whether the rule applies beyond the advertised area.

A spreadsheet can generate a table from a model. Put x values in column A and, for C=600x+1500, enter =600*A2+1500 in B2 if the first distance is in A2. Copy the formula down so each row refers to its own distance. Use an XY scatter chart because both coordinates are numerical. Label both axes with units; a category chart can conceal unequal distance intervals.

To compare two charges, calculate both costs for the same x values. An intersection represents equal costs. A display window can hide an intersection or make nearby lines appear identical. Zoom sensibly, inspect numerical coordinates and substitute the proposed point into both original rules. Software gives evidence; an algebraic equality gives an exact solution for linear rules.

A model is useful only within its assumptions. A negative distance solution has no meaning for a delivery journey. A bus count must be a whole number even if a graph allows fractions. Rounding can alter a comparison near an intersection, so retain exact values until the final decision. Record the formulas, units and allowed range so someone else can reproduce the investigation.
examples: A bicycle courier charges C=400x+1200. At x=3.5 km, C=400×3.5+1200=2600 shillings. The rate is 400 shillings/km and the fixed charge is 1200 shillings.

Compare A=300x+1800 with B=500x+1000. Equal costs give 300x+1800=500x+1000, hence 800=200x and x=4 km. Both cost 3000 shillings. At 2 km A costs 2400 and B 2000, so B is cheaper below 4 km within the model.
A spreadsheet uses distances 0, 2, 5 km. For y=2x+1 the outputs are 1, 5, 11. An XY scatter chart plots (0,1), (2,5), (5,11) with unequal horizontal gaps; the gradient is (11−1)/(5−0)=2.

glossary.definition: A mathematical description based on stated assumptions.
A chart that positions each point by two numerical coordinates.

chapters.title: Rates, direct and inverse variation
objectives: Distinguish a rate from a ratio
Find constants of direct and inverse variation
Test a model before using it for prediction
paragraphs: A rate compares quantities with different units, such as litres per minute or shillings per kilogram. Divide the amount by the corresponding number of units. Conversion must preserve the same physical quantity: 72 km/h is 72000 m in 3600 s, or 20 m/s. A unit rate makes fair comparisons possible when packages or journey times differ.

Direct variation means y=kx for a constant k. The ratio y/x is constant for nonzero x, and its graph is a straight line through the origin. Doubling x doubles y. A straight line with a nonzero intercept is a linear relationship but is not direct variation; a fixed service fee is one reason a cost does not vary directly with usage.

Inverse variation means y=k/x, so xy=k for nonzero x. Doubling x halves y. For a fixed job, the time may vary inversely with the number of equally productive workers, provided they can work independently without delays. Real teams may not satisfy these assumptions. The graph is a curve, and x=0 is excluded.

Variation can also involve powers or two inputs: y=kx² or y=kx/z. Determine k using one complete set of data, then retain it when substituting new inputs. Check units and whether a prediction is sensible. Two isolated measurements that look proportional do not prove a universal physical law; further measurements should test the proposed model.
examples: A tap fills 42 L in 3 minutes at a steady rate. Rate=42/3=14 L/min. In 8 minutes it fills 14×8=112 L, assuming the flow remains steady.
If y varies directly as x and y=35 when x=5, k=35/5=7. Thus y=7x; when x=12, y=84. The ratio stays 7.
Six equally productive workers finish a fixed task in 10 days. Under an inverse model nt=60 worker-days. With 15 workers, t=60/15=4 days; the prediction assumes no interference or change in hours.

glossary.definition: A relationship y=kx with constant ratio y/x.
A relationship y=k/x with constant product xy.
The fixed multiplier k in a variation model.

chapters.title: Similarity and scale factors
objectives: Match corresponding sides and angles
Use length, area and volume scale factors
Measure inaccessible lengths with explicit assumptions
paragraphs: Similar shapes have the same shape: corresponding angles are equal and corresponding lengths are in a constant ratio. Name corresponding vertices in the same order. If triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF, AB corresponds to DE, BC to EF, and AC to DF. A scale factor from the first shape to the second is a second-shape length divided by its corresponding first-shape length.

Triangles can be shown similar by two equal corresponding angles (AA), three proportional corresponding sides (SSS similarity), or two proportional sides with equal included angle (SAS similarity). A visual resemblance is not proof. Parallel lines often create equal corresponding or alternate angles, allowing a similarity argument before any length calculation.

If lengths scale by k, areas scale by k² and volumes of similar solids scale by k³. These are different multipliers. A drawing twice as wide and twice as high covers four times the area. Units remain essential: a map scale 1:25000 compares lengths in the same units, so 1 cm represents 25000 cm, or 250 m.

Shadow measurements can estimate height using similar right triangles when objects stand vertically on level ground and sunlight reaches both at the same angle at the same time. Divide height by shadow length for the reference object and apply the same ratio. Uneven ground, leaning objects and measurements taken at different times weaken the model. Never enter roads or climb structures to measure them.
examples: Triangle sides 3,4,5 cm correspond to 9,12,15 cm. Each ratio is 3, so the triangles are similar with scale factor 3. Their area ratio is 3²=9.
A 1.5 m vertical pole casts a 2 m shadow while a tree casts an 8 m shadow on level ground. h/8=1.5/2, so h=6 m under the shared-angle assumption.
On a 1:40000 map a path measures 3.2 cm. Actual length=3.2×40000=128000 cm=1280 m=1.28 km.

chapters.title: Congruent triangles and proof
objectives: Select valid congruence tests
Write a correspondence-based proof
Distinguish congruence evidence from similarity evidence
paragraphs: Congruent figures have the same shape and size. A rotation, reflection or translation can move one onto the other without stretching. In triangles, proving congruence allows us to conclude that all corresponding sides and angles are equal. A correct vertex correspondence is necessary before making these conclusions.

The SSS test uses equality of all three corresponding sides. SAS uses equality of two sides and the angle included between them. ASA uses two corresponding angles and the side between them; two angles also determine the third angle, so an appropriate AAS argument works as well. For right triangles, RHS uses a right angle, equal hypotenuses and one equal corresponding leg.

AAA shows shape but does not determine size: triangles with sides 3,4,5 and 6,8,10 have equal angles but are not congruent. Two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) do not provide a general congruence rule, because different triangles can satisfy such information. Identify where an angle lies instead of choosing a test from a count of marks alone.

A proof separates facts, reasons and conclusions. Given equal lengths may be combined with a common side, vertically opposite angles or angles established by parallel lines. State a test, list the triangle correspondence, then use corresponding parts. A diagram supports reasoning but cannot certify a length or angle merely because it looks equal.

chapters.title: Binary operations and algebraic structure
objectives: Evaluate an explicitly defined operation
Test closure, commutativity and associativity
Find an identity and an inverse when they exist
paragraphs: A binary operation combines two elements of a stated set to produce one result. The symbol is a label whose meaning must be defined: if a★b=2a+b, then 3★4=10. It is not ordinary multiplication. Substitute the first input for a and the second for b, keeping their positions and using brackets when an input is negative or is itself an expression.

Closure means the result stays in the stated set for every allowed pair. Subtraction is closed on integers but not on nonnegative integers, because 2−5=−3. Division on real numbers cannot accept a zero second input. Always state the domain before declaring that a rule is an operation on a set; the same formula may work on one set and fail on another.

An operation is commutative if a★b=b★a for every allowed pair. It is associative if (a★b)★c=a★(b★c) for every allowed triple. A counterexample disproves a universal claim, but one matching numerical example does not prove it. Compare general expressions where possible. Associativity controls regrouping; commutativity controls order.

An identity e satisfies a★e=e★a=a for all a. An inverse of a, relative to identity e, is an element b with a★b=b★a=e. Solve these conditions using the defined rule and then check membership of the result in the set. A rule may have no two-sided identity, and without a specified identity the usual inverse question is not meaningful.
examples: For a★b=2a+b, 4★(−3)=2×4−3=5. But (−3)★4=−6+4=−2, so this operation on real numbers is not commutative.
Define a∘b=a+b+2 on integers. Then (a∘b)∘c=a+b+c+4=a∘(b∘c), so it is associative. An identity satisfies a+e+2=a, giving e=−2, which also works on the left.
For a∘b=a+b+2 with identity −2, the inverse of 5 solves 5+b+2=−2, giving b=−9. Check 5∘(−9)=−2 and (−9)∘5=−2.

chapters.title: Logarithms as inverse powers
objectives: Convert between exponential and logarithmic statements
Apply logarithm laws with valid domains
Solve and check elementary logarithmic equations
paragraphs: For base b>0 and b≠1, log_b(x)=y means b^y=x, with x>0. A logarithm asks for an exponent. Since 10³=1000, log₁₀(1000)=3. The common logarithm uses base 10. A real logarithm of zero or a negative number is undefined; negative logarithm values are allowed when the positive argument is between zero and one and the base exceeds one.

For positive M and N, log_b(MN)=log_b M+log_b N and log_b(M/N)=log_b M−log_b N. These laws come from adding and subtracting exponents. They do not turn a sum inside a logarithm into a sum of logarithms: log_b(M+N) generally has no such split. Keep the base fixed throughout a law application.

The power law is log_b(M^r)=r log_b M for positive M and real r. In particular log_b 1=0 and log_b b=1. When using a calculator, enter brackets around the full argument and round only at the end. If a calculator only has common logarithms, log_b x=log₁₀ x/log₁₀ b, with b valid and x positive.

Solve logarithmic equations by respecting domains first, applying laws or converting to exponential form, and checking the original expressions at the end. Algebra may produce a value that makes an original argument nonpositive. Such a value must be rejected even if it satisfies an equation obtained after transformation.
examples: log₂ 32 asks for y with 2^y=32. Since 2⁵=32, y=5. Similarly log₁₀ 0.01=−2 because 10^(−2)=0.01.
Evaluate log₃ 27+log₃ 9−log₃ 3. The values are 3+2−1=4. Equivalently combine the arguments: log₃(27×9/3)=log₃ 81=4.
Solve log₁₀(x−1)+log₁₀(x+1)=log₁₀ 8. Domain x>1. Combine to obtain (x−1)(x+1)=8, so x²=9 and x=±3. Only x=3 is valid; its arguments are 2 and 4 with product 8.

chapters.title: Radicals and rational denominators
objectives: Simplify radicals using square factors
Combine and multiply radical expressions
Rationalise simple and binomial denominators
paragraphs: The principal square root √a is the nonnegative number whose square is a, for a≥0. Thus √25=5, while solving x²=25 gives x=5 or x=−5. For real x, √(x²)=|x|. These statements prevent a common sign error when variables might be negative.

For nonnegative a and b, √(ab)=√a√b. Factor out a perfect square to simplify a radical: √72=√(36×2)=6√2. Only like radicals combine by addition or subtraction, just as like algebraic terms combine. The rule √(a+b)=√a+√b is generally false; test a=b=1 to see √2 differs from 2.

Multiply radicals using distribution and simplify each resulting term. A conjugate pair has the form p+q and p−q; their product p²−q² removes the middle terms. In particular, (√a+√b)(√a−√b)=a−b when both square roots are real. Check that a proposed denominator is nonzero before manipulating a fraction.

Rationalising a denominator rewrites an equivalent fraction with no radical in that denominator. Multiply numerator and denominator by the same nonzero expression. For 1/√a with a>0, multiply by √a/√a. For a denominator √a+√b, its conjugate may remove the radicals. chapters.title: Floating, sinking and displaced water
objectives: Relate upthrust to displaced liquid
Predict floating using average density
Test and improve a safe floating prototype
paragraphs: A liquid exerts pressure on every submerged surface. Pressure increases with depth, so the upward force on the lower parts of an object exceeds the downward force on its upper parts. The resultant upward fluid force is upthrust. Archimedes' principle states that the upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced by the object: U=ρgV, where V is the submerged volume, not necessarily the whole object volume.

A freely floating object at rest has balanced vertical forces: upthrust equals its total weight. A fully submerged object released from rest sinks if its weight exceeds the upthrust, rises if upthrust exceeds weight, and can remain neutrally buoyant if they balance. Comparing average object density with fluid density gives the same prediction when trapped air and all parts are included in the average.

A solid steel block sinks in water, but a hollow steel boat can float because the mass of steel and enclosed air is spread over a larger external volume. A floating boat displaces its own weight of water. Adding cargo makes it settle deeper until it displaces more water; if water enters and displaces the enclosed air, its average density increases and it may sink. Stability also matters, so a floating design is not automatically safe for carrying people.

Test a small foil boat in a shallow tray on a stable table. Use counters or washers as cargo, add them slowly near the centre, record total supported mass and compare different hull shapes made from equal foil areas. Keep electrical equipment away and dry spilled water. These are tabletop models; never use a student prototype to support a person or enter deep water. Use g=10 N/kg and water density 1000 kg/m³ in this chapter unless stated otherwise.
examples: A submerged block displaces 0.002 m³ of water. U=1000×10×0.002=20 N. If its weight is 30 N, the initial resultant force is 30−20=10 N downward, so it sinks when released.
A 0.6 kg object floats. Its weight is 0.6×10=6 N, so U=6 N. Displaced volume V=6/(1000×10)=0.0006 m³=600 cm³.
A uniform block has density 750 kg/m³ and floats in water. From ρ_water g V_sub=ρ_block g V_total, V_sub/V_total=750/1000=0.75. Therefore 75% of its volume is submerged and 25% remains above water.

chapters.title: Mechanical properties and spring investigations
objectives: Distinguish elasticity, plasticity and stiffness
Use Hooke’s law within its limits
Calibrate a safe spring-based measuring prototype
paragraphs: Materials respond differently to forces. An elastic material returns to its original dimensions after unloading within its elastic range. Plastic deformation remains after unloading. Stiffness describes resistance to deformation: a stiffer spring extends less for the same force. Strength concerns resistance to failure, while brittleness concerns fracture with little plastic deformation; these are not synonyms for stiffness.

For a spring obeying Hooke's law, F=kx, where F is applied force in newtons, x is extension in metres and k is spring constant in N/m. Extension is loaded length minus original length, not the total spring length. The law applies only over the proportional range; increasing a load indefinitely can permanently stretch or break the spring.

A force-versus-extension graph is straight through the origin in the Hooke's-law range. Its gradient ΔF/Δx is k. If extension is plotted vertically instead, the gradient is 1/k, so read axis labels before interpreting a slope. Elastic energy stored in an ideal Hooke's-law spring is E=½Fx=½kx², equal to the triangular area under its force–extension graph during loading.

A simple force-meter prototype can use a teacher-approved spring, a paper scale and small known masses. Clamp it securely, place a tray below the masses and keep faces away from suspended loads. Add loads gradually, record extensions on loading and unloading, and stop at the approved maximum. Recheck the zero after removal of loads; a shifted zero may reveal permanent deformation and invalidate calibration. Use g=10 N/kg for numerical work here.
examples: An unloaded spring is 8 cm long and reaches 11 cm under 1.5 N. Extension=3 cm=0.03 m. Thus k=1.5/0.03=50 N/m; using 11 cm as extension would be wrong.
For k=80 N/m and load 2.4 N, x=F/k=2.4/80=0.03 m=3 cm. This prediction is valid only if the load is in the spring's proportional range.
A spring with k=200 N/m extends 0.04 m. Force=200×0.04=8 N. Stored energy=½×200×0.04²=0.16 J, the same as ½×8×0.04.

chapters.title: Magnets, fields and a compass prototype
objectives: Describe poles and magnetic fields
Explain magnetisation and demagnetisation
Collect evidence using a safe compass prototype
paragraphs: A magnet has north-seeking and south-seeking poles. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Some materials, notably iron and many steels, can be magnetised; many other metals such as aluminium and copper are not strongly attracted by an ordinary school magnet. Attraction alone does not prove that an unknown object is already a magnet because unmagnetised iron is also attracted. Repulsion from a known pole is stronger evidence of an existing magnetic pole.

A magnetic field is a region where magnetic forces can act. A small compass indicates the local field direction through its north-seeking end. Outside a bar magnet, field lines are drawn from north to south; closer spacing represents a stronger field. Field lines do not cross because the field has one direction at each point. The lines are a model, not physical strings inside the space.

A domain model explains magnetisation by increased alignment of many small magnetic regions. Stroking a steel needle repeatedly in one direction with one pole can align it sufficiently for a compass demonstration; lift the magnet away on each return stroke. Soft iron magnetises and loses magnetism readily, while steel often retains it better. Heating or mechanical shock can disrupt alignment, but learners should not heat, strike or damage magnets in class. Storage with suitable keepers helps preserve some bar magnets.

A teacher can prepare a magnetised needle and secure it flat on a small cork disk floating in a shallow tray, with its sharp point covered. Away from magnets and steel furniture it turns approximately north–south in Earth's field. Compare its direction with a known compass before labelling the ends. Record repeated headings, disturbances and limitations; nearby magnetic materials can distort readings. Keep small magnets away from mouths, electronic devices and medical implants; use a commercial compass when a needle prototype is unsuitable.

chapters.title: Static charge, conductors and capacitors
objectives: Explain charge transfer and induction
Distinguish conductors, insulators and earthing
Interpret electroscope evidence and basic capacitor quantities
paragraphs: Static electricity concerns electric charge that accumulates rather than flowing steadily around a circuit. Atoms contain positive nuclei and negative electrons. In ordinary rubbing experiments electrons transfer between materials; protons do not move from object to object. An object gaining electrons becomes negatively charged and one losing electrons becomes positively charged. Rubbing separates charge rather than creating a net supply of it.

Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. A charged object can also attract a neutral object by polarisation: opposite charge is displaced slightly closer than like charge. In a conductor, some electrons move readily; an insulator restricts large-scale electron movement. Charging by contact transfers charge, while induction can redistribute charge without touching. Earthing connects an object to the Earth so electrons can move in the direction required by the electrical conditions.

An electroscope can show the presence of charge through separation of similarly charged leaves. An initially uncharged electroscope's divergence alone does not reveal whether the nearby charge is positive or negative. A known initial charge and controlled procedure are needed to compare signs. On an isolated conducting body at electrostatic equilibrium, excess charge lies on its outer surface; sharp regions can produce stronger nearby fields. A lightning protection system provides an engineered path to earth; its installation is professional work.

A capacitor stores separated charge on two conductors separated by an insulator. Its capacitance C=Q/V measures stored charge magnitude per potential difference; the SI unit is the farad (F), with Q in coulombs and V in volts. A capacitor has equal and opposite plate charges rather than a net charge Q on the whole ideal device. Study school-approved low-voltage components only: never open mains appliances or handle unknown charged capacitors. Static demonstrations should use dry plastic and paper, away from flammable vapours and electronic equipment.
examples: A plastic ruler gains electrons when rubbed. It becomes negatively charged; the other material loses the same number of electrons and becomes positive. The total charge of the isolated pair remains unchanged.

A charged balloon attracts a neutral wall. The wall's charges shift slightly, making the nearer region effectively opposite in sign. Attraction therefore does not prove the wall carried an opposite net charge before the balloon approached.
A capacitor stores charge magnitude Q=0.000024 C at V=12 V. C=Q/V=0.000002 F=2 μF. If the same ideal capacitor is used at 6 V, Q=CV=0.000012 C=12 μC.

chapters.title: Optical instruments and experimental design
objectives: Explain a pinhole camera, simple magnifier and periscope
Use magnification ratios with units
Analyse optical data and communicate a prototype test
paragraphs: An optical instrument controls light to make an image or redirect a view. In a pinhole camera, rays travel approximately straight from the top and bottom of an object through a small hole to opposite parts of a screen, producing a real inverted image. A smaller hole can sharpen the image but reduces brightness; making it extremely small introduces diffraction, so smaller is not always better. A dark enclosure reduces unwanted light.

A simple magnifier uses a converging lens with the object inside its focal length. The emerging rays diverge and the eye traces them back to an upright, magnified virtual image. A camera lens instead forms a real image on a sensor or screen when the object is beyond the focal length. A real image can be received on a screen; a virtual image cannot be projected directly there. Never view the Sun or intense light through any optical instrument.

A simple periscope uses two parallel plane mirrors, commonly placed at 45° to the tube direction. Two successive reflections redirect rays around an obstruction. The law of reflection applies at each mirror: angles are measured from the normal. Aligning and securing the mirrors matters more than decorating the housing. Teacher-provided unbroken mirrors or suitable mirror sheet should be used; learners should not cut glass.

For a pinhole camera viewing a perpendicular object, similar triangles give image height/object height=image distance/object distance, using positive magnitudes. Measure all lengths in compatible units. A spreadsheet can hold object distance, image distance and image height, calculate ratios, and display a labelled XY graph. Repeat measurements and report their spread; compare a prediction with observations rather than inventing perfect data. An oral report should state the question, method, evidence, conclusion and limitations. Safe bright classroom objects or an LED target may be used, never the Sun.
examples: A 30 cm high object is 150 cm from a pinhole and the screen is 10 cm behind it. Image height/30=10/150, so image height=2 cm. The image is inverted and real.
A camera image is 8 mm high for an object 400 mm high. Linear magnification magnitude=8/400=0.02. The small image does not imply poor focus; size and sharpness are different observations.

At fixed object distance 200 cm and object height 40 cm, screen distances 5,10,15 cm predict image heights 1,2,3 cm. A plot of image height against screen distance is a line through the origin with gradient 40/200=0.2, using the same length units for both axes.
